title: Starting a Hospice Program in Kansas: Licensing, Costs, and Step-by-Step Guide

Introduction

Starting a Hospice Program in Kansas represents a meaningful opportunity to serve individuals requiring end-of-life care while building a compliant, sustainable care business. Oversight and state-level coordination are administered by the Kansas Department of Health and Environment (KDHE), but the primary operational framework is achieving and maintaining Medicare certification through the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS). Reimbursement and program funding are coordinated through CMS and the Kansas Medical Assistance Program (KMAP) where applicable.

With provider capacity generally meeting demand and significant federal grant support for rural health, Kansas offers a stable market for providers prepared to navigate the rigorous requirements of Medicare certification, staffing, and compliance. Reimbursement rates, which range from approximately $190 to over $600 per day depending on the level of care, create a viable financial model for agencies that manage operations effectively.

This guide walks you through every step of launching a Hospice Program in Kansas, from understanding federal regulations and state oversight to staffing your interdisciplinary team, managing reimbursement, and preparing for certification surveys.

Table of Contents

  • Understand Kansas’s Hospice Program Regulations
  • Choose the Type and Size of Your Program
  • Business Structure and Licensing
  • Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan
  • Secure a Suitable Facility or Office
  • Hire and Train Qualified Staff
  • Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans
  • Marketing and Referral Development
  • Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews
  • Frequently Asked Questions

Section 1: Understand Kansas’s Hospice Program Regulations

Kansas regulates Hospice Programs through the Kansas Department of Health and Environment (KDHE), which is primarily responsible for conducting certification surveys on behalf of the federal government. The core of hospice regulation is not a state-specific license but rather achieving and maintaining Medicare certification. This means your agency’s operations, policies, and clinical practices must align with the federal CMS Conditions of Participation (CoPs) for hospice care.

Providers serving Medicaid-eligible populations must also comply with rules set by the Kansas Medical Assistance Program (KMAP), which generally aligns its requirements and reimbursement with Medicare. Additionally, all operations must adhere to federal frameworks like the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) to protect patient information.

The regulatory framework emphasizes a patient-and-family-centered model of care, focusing on key themes like comprehensive patient assessment, interdisciplinary care planning, pain and symptom management, and patient rights. Medicare certification is not a one-time event; it is an ongoing status maintained through periodic recertification surveys, typically occurring every 36 months, or more frequently if complaints are filed or deficiencies are found. Your agency must be in a constant state of readiness.

Section 2: Choose the Type and Size of Your Program

While you will operate under a single Hospice Program certification, Kansas and CMS recognize four distinct levels of care. Your agency must have the capability to provide and bill for each, as patient needs dictate. These levels of care function as the primary service variants:

  • Routine Home Care (RHC): The most common level of care, where services are provided in the patient’s place of residence, whether that is a private home, assisted living facility, or nursing home.
  • Continuous Home Care (CHC): Provided during periods of crisis to manage acute medical symptoms. This involves skilled nursing care in the home for a minimum of 8 hours in a 24-hour period to keep the patient at home.
  • General Inpatient Care (GIP): Short-term care provided in a Medicare-certified facility (hospital, skilled nursing facility, or inpatient hospice unit) for pain or symptom management that cannot be handled in another setting.
  • Inpatient Respite Care: Short-term care provided in a facility to relieve family members or other caregivers. This is limited to five consecutive days at a time.

Program size is measured by Average Daily Census (ADC). A new agency might start by building a caseload of 10-20 patients and grow to an ADC of 50 or more. Demand is consistent in urban centers like Wichita, Overland Park, and Kansas City, which have many established providers. However, significant opportunities exist in rural counties, which are a focus of federal grant support and may have fewer dedicated hospice providers, representing a chance to enter the market with less direct competition.

Section 3: Business Structure and Licensing

Before you can serve patients, you must establish a formal business entity. Providers in Kansas typically operate as a Limited Liability Company (LLC) or a Corporation (S-Corp or C-Corp) for liability protection. The foundational steps include:

  • Register your business name and entity with the Kansas Secretary of State.
  • Obtain an Employer Identification Number (EIN) from the IRS for tax purposes.
  • Secure required insurance coverage, including general liability, professional liability (malpractice), and workers’ compensation.
  • Submit a Medicare certification application (Form CMS-855A) and register with KDHE to initiate the survey process.

Obtaining Medicare certification is the most critical and time-consuming part of the process. The licensing and certification timeline in Kansas generally ranges from 4 to 8 months. This timeframe depends heavily on the completeness of your application, your readiness for the on-site survey, and the scheduling availability of the state surveyors.

Section 4: Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan

A robust business plan is essential for securing funding and guiding your launch. Startup costs for a hospice agency in Kansas typically range from $75,000 to $150,000. This initial investment covers expenses such as business registration, licensing and accreditation fees, office rent and setup, initial staff salaries, electronic medical record (EMR) software, and marketing.

Operating expenses are driven primarily by payroll. Staffing represents approximately 60-70% of total costs in a service-based hospice model. Your financial projections must be based on realistic reimbursement rates. A typical revenue snapshot in Kansas includes:

  • Routine Home Care (RHC): Approximately $190+ per day
  • Continuous Home Care (CHC): Billed hourly, often exceeding $50 per hour, which can total over $1,200 for a 24-hour period.
  • Inpatient Respite Care: Approximately $200+ per day
  • General Inpatient Care (GIP): Approximately $750+ per day

Profitability in hospice is a function of managing your patient census and controlling costs. Most agencies need to reach a target Average Daily Census (ADC) of 15-25 patients to achieve break-even and begin generating profit. With efficient operations, providers can achieve the national average of approximately 8% profit margins.

Section 5: Secure a Suitable Facility or Office

Unlike an assisted living facility, a hospice agency does not require a large residential building. Your primary physical location is an administrative office that serves as the hub for your interdisciplinary team. This office must meet professional standards and local regulations. Key facility requirements include:

  • An administrative office that complies with local zoning and building codes.
  • A secure, locked area for storing patient records to ensure HIPAA compliance.
  • A conference room or dedicated space for interdisciplinary group (IDG) meetings, staff training, and family consultations.
  • Accessibility for individuals with disabilities in accordance with the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA).
  • Sufficient parking for your administrative and clinical staff.

When selecting a location, consider its proximity to major referral sources like hospitals and skilled nursing facilities, as well as its accessibility for your workforce. A central location can reduce travel time for your field staff and improve operational efficiency.

Section 6: Hire and Train Qualified Staff

The heart of a hospice program is its interdisciplinary group (IDG). CMS regulations mandate a specific team structure, and hiring qualified, compassionate professionals is non-negotiable. Required roles in Kansas typically include:

  • Medical Director: A physician (MD or DO) who provides medical oversight and direction for the program.
  • Administrator: An experienced healthcare manager responsible for the day-to-day operations of the agency.
  • Director of Nursing (DON): A Registered Nurse (RN) with at least two years of hospice or related experience who manages all clinical staff and services.
  • Clinical Staff: Registered Nurses (RNs) and Licensed Practical Nurses (LPNs) with active Kansas licenses to provide direct patient care.
  • Social Workers: Licensed Master Social Workers (LMSW) to provide psychosocial support to patients and families.
  • Home Health Aides: Certified aides who have completed a 75-hour training program and passed a competency evaluation.
  • Spiritual Care Coordinator/Chaplain: To address the spiritual needs of patients and families.
  • Volunteer Coordinator & Volunteers: CMS requires that volunteer hours equal at least 5% of total patient care hours.

All staff must undergo thorough background checks. Training is a critical component of compliance. Beyond the initial 75 hours for aides, all clinical staff must complete 12 hours of annual continuing education relevant to hospice and palliative care. This training should cover topics like pain management, communication, and the latest regulatory updates.

Section 7: Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans

To pass your Medicare certification survey, you must have a comprehensive set of written policies and procedures that govern every aspect of your operation. These documents are the blueprint for your agency and prove to surveyors that you have a plan for providing compliant, high-quality care. Kansas and CMS require written policies covering:

  • Patient Rights and Responsibilities
  • Interdisciplinary Group (IDG) Management and Communication
  • Comprehensive Patient Assessment Process
  • Plan of Care Development, Review, and Updates
  • Pain and Symptom Management Protocols
  • Infection Control and Prevention
  • Emergency Preparedness Plan
  • Volunteer Program Management and Training
  • Bereavement Services for Families
  • Quality Assessment and Performance Improvement (QAPI) Program

Individualized plans of care are the cornerstone of hospice. Each plan must be developed by the IDG in collaboration with the patient and family, reviewed at least every 15 days, and meticulously documented to reflect the patient’s evolving needs and goals.

Section 8: Marketing and Referral Development

Hospice marketing is not about direct-to-consumer advertising. Success is built on professional relationships and a reputation for quality and responsiveness. Your marketing efforts should be a B2B (business-to-business) strategy focused on developing a strong network of referral sources. In Kansas, referrals typically come from:

  • Hospitals: Specifically discharge planners, case managers, and palliative care teams.
  • Oncologists and other specialists who treat patients with life-limiting illnesses.
  • Skilled Nursing Facilities (SNFs): For long-term residents who become hospice-appropriate.
  • Assisted Living Facilities: As a partner to provide a higher level of care for their residents.
  • Primary Care Physicians who manage the long-term care of their patients.
  • Home Health Agencies that transition patients from curative to palliative care.

Build trust with these partners by being highly responsive, providing excellent clinical communication, and demonstrating positive patient outcomes. Your compliance and quality of care are your best marketing tools.

Section 9: Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews

Oversight in Kansas is conducted by state surveyors from KDHE acting on behalf of CMS. These on-site inspections, or surveys, are unannounced and focus on ensuring your agency is adhering to the CMS Conditions of Participation. Surveyors will review patient charts, interview staff and families, and may even accompany nurses on home visits.

Common deficiencies cited during hospice surveys often relate to documentation and process failures. Be prepared to avoid:

  • Incomplete or outdated Plans of Care that do not reflect the patient’s current condition.
  • Lack of documented Interdisciplinary Group (IDG) meetings or failure to show all disciplines participated.
  • Inadequate documentation of pain and symptom management interventions and outcomes.
  • Failure to meet the 5% volunteer hour requirement.
  • Issues with aide supervision, including lack of documented RN supervisory visits.

Maintaining a state of continuous survey readiness is essential. Implement a robust Quality Assessment and Performance Improvement (QAPI) program to constantly self-audit your processes, identify potential issues, and correct them before a surveyor finds them.

Section 10: Frequently Asked Questions

Q: How long does it take to open a Hospice Program in Kansas?

  • A: The entire process, from business formation to passing your Medicare certification survey, typically takes 4 to 8 months. The timeline can be influenced by the completeness of your application, your team’s readiness, and the state’s survey schedule.

Q: What licenses are required to start a hospice in Kansas?

  • A: The primary requirement is not a traditional state license but Medicare certification, which is granted after a successful survey conducted by the Kansas Department of Health and Environment (KDHE) on behalf of CMS. You will also need standard business licenses from your local city and county.

Q: What reimbursement is available for hospice services in Kansas?

  • A: Reimbursement primarily comes from the Medicare hospice benefit and is paid on a per diem (per day) basis. Rates vary by the level of care provided, ranging from approximately $190 for routine home care to over $600 for more intensive levels like continuous or inpatient care. Kansas Medicaid (KMAP) and most private insurers generally align their rates with the Medicare fee schedule.

Conclusion

Starting a Hospice Program in Kansas is a complex but deeply rewarding venture. It requires careful planning, a deep understanding of federal regulations, and a steadfast commitment to operational discipline. Providers who invest in building a strong interdisciplinary team, maintaining meticulous compliance with CMS Conditions of Participation, and cultivating strong referral relationships are positioned for long-term success and the privilege of providing comfort and dignity to patients at the end of life.
